from nsp_grok.commands import dispatch
from nsp_grok.lab import Store


def _admin_ctx():
    store = Store()
    return build_ctx(store, store.users["admin"])


def _viewer_ctx():
    store = Store()
    return build_ctx(store, store.users["viewer"])


def test_ls_root():
    ctx = _admin_ctx()
    out = dispatch(ctx, "ls")
    assert out.error == ""
    assert out.renderable is not None


def test_cd_show_ne():
    ctx = _admin_ctx()
    dispatch(ctx, "cd /equipment/METRO-BA/PE-BAIRES-01")
    out = dispatch(ctx, "show")
    assert out.error == ""


def test_mpls_lsp_list():
    ctx = _admin_ctx()
    out = dispatch(ctx, "/mpls lsps")
    assert out.error == ""


def test_create_and_shutdown_lsp():
    ctx = _admin_ctx()
    out = dispatch(
        ctx,
        "mpls lsp create name=lsp-test from=PE-BAIRES-01 to=PE-CORDOBA-01 type=dynamic sig=rsvp",
    )
    assert out.error == ""
    assert "lsp-test" in ctx.store.lsps
    out = dispatch(ctx, "mpls lsp shutdown lsp-test")
    assert ctx.store.lsps["lsp-test"].admin == "down"


def test_viewer_cannot_create_lsp():
    ctx = _viewer_ctx()
    out = dispatch(
        ctx,
        "mpls lsp create name=lsp-x from=PE-BAIRES-01 to=PE-CORDOBA-01",
    )
    assert "permission denied" in out.error


def test_alarm_ack():
    ctx = _admin_ctx()
    out = dispatch(ctx, "alarm ack A-1001")

    assert alarm.acked
    assert alarm.acked_by == "admin"

    out = dispatch(ctx, "blargh")
    assert "unknown command" in out.error

    ctx = _admin_ctx()
    out = dispatch(ctx, "find BAIRES")
    assert out.error == ""

```powershell
cd C:\Users\elzoy\Code\nsp-grok-2411

python -m nsp_grok

```
admin / › ls

124→receive near-real-time Kafka event notifications. See theNetwork Developer Portalfor information.

126→Note: The NSP REST APIs also allow OSS clients to integrate with other NSP components.

238→3.4 Secure communication
239→
240→3.4.1 Overview
241→The XML API provides the following functions for secure communication between the OSS clients
242→and the NFM-P:
243→• MD5-hashed passwords for requests
244→• TLS message encryption for JMS events
245→• HTTPS for XML requests and responses
246→
247→Note: MD5-hashed passwords do not secure the communication channel.
248→
249→Note: Nokia recommends enabling TLS for secure communication.
250→
251→TLS is enabled by default on NFM-P server and client interfaces to provide secure communication
252→between NFM-P components. TLS requires a security certificate that is shared among members of
253→a network domain using TLS keystore and truststore files. The NFM-P supports using CA-supplied
254→or self-signed certificates.
255→
256→For backward compatibility, the NFM-P supports non-secure communication with OSS clients. To
257→support non-secure clients, you must disable TLS on the XML API.
258→
259→Note: Disabling TLS on the XML API disables TLS for all clients that use the XML API, and for
260→all NFM-P GUI clients. Browser-based clients are unaffected, and must use HTTPS for
261→application access.
262→
263→See the NSP Installation and Upgrade Guide for information about configuring NFM-P TLS.

291→location of the truststore file on the OSS client station. For more information, see the TLS

3 Communicating with the 


3.1 Overview

3.1.1 Overview
The following communication mechanisms are available to NFM-P OSS clients:
• NFM-P XML API and JMS event stream
• NSP REST API and Kafka notification service

The XML API receives SOAP XML requests for configuring and managing NFM-P system and
network objects. The XML JMS event stream allows OSS clients to receive near-real-time
notification of NFM-P system and managed-network events. The NSP NFM-P XML API Developer
Guide focuses primarily on OSS application integration with the XML API and JMS mechanisms.

By subscribing to NSP REST APIs, an NFM-P OSS client can configure and manage objects, and
receive near-real-time Kafka event notifications. See theNetwork Developer Portalfor information.

Note: The NSP REST APIs also allow OSS clients to integrate with other NSP components.

A developer who creates an OSS application for the XML API requires knowledge of the following:
• standard XML schema constructions
• OSS interfaces
• managed devices
• NFM-P functions

3.2 NFM-P system components

3.2.1 Overview
An NFM-P system has multiple components. The components are briefly described 1.1 in“NFM-P
product overview” (p. 13). For a comprehensive description of NFM-P system components and
relationships, see the Component communication information in the NSP Architecture Guide .

3.3.2 Event monitoring using JMS
Clients can monitor events in the NFM-P and the network by subscribing to event streams. This
event-driven function allows a client to maintain a near-real-time view of events in the network.
However, the function is unidirectional and does not allow clients to initiate changes in the NFM-P

3.3.4 XML and SOAP
The JMS events and HTTP requests and responses are written in XML using the SOAP standard.
XML is a standard format used to describe data. The Schema Reference is defined in XML style
sheets, which are distributed with the documentation. API requests and responses, and JMS events
are wrapped in SOAP envelopes.

For more information, see the related W3C specifications and other related material available from
technical publishers and the Internet. Some suggested resources are:
• http://www.w3.org/XML
• http://www.w3.org/TR/soap
• Ray, Eric T. Learning XML (2nd Ed). O’Reilly, 2003

3.4 Secure communication

3.4.1 Overview
The XML API provides the following functions for secure communication between the OSS clients
and the NFM-P:
• MD5-hashed passwords for requests
• TLS message encryption for JMS events
• HTTPS for XML requests and responses

Note: MD5-hashed passwords do not secure the communication channel.

Note: Nokia recommends enabling TLS for secure communication.

TLS is enabled by default on NFM-P server and client interfaces to provide secure communication
between NFM-P components. TLS requires a security certificate that is shared among members of
a network domain using TLS keystore and truststore files. The NFM-P supports using CA-supplied
or self-signed certificates.

For backward compatibility, the NFM-P supports non-secure communication with OSS clients. To
support non-secure clients, you must disable TLS on the XML API.

Note: Disabling TLS on the XML API disables TLS for all clients that use the XML API, and for
all NFM-P GUI clients. Browser-based clients are unaffected, and must use HTTPS for
application access.

See the NSP Installation and Upgrade Guide for information about configuring NFM-P TLS.

3.4.2 TLS communication
When establishing TLS communication from an OSS system, an NFM-P main server selects the
highest security cipher that the OSS client presents. The specific set of supported security ciphers
and algorithms may vary, depending on the OSS client and server software components and
certificates.

You can use an NFM-P tool to specify which TLS versions and ciphers the NFM-P supports. See
the procedure to update the supported NFM-P TLS versions and ciphers in NSP the System
Administrator Guide for information about using the tool.

3.5 TLS message encryption

3.5.1 Overview
OSS clients can receive secure JMS XML messages using TLS encryption. To enable TLS for an
OSS client, you must import a TLS certificate from an NFM-P main server to a TLS truststore file on
the OSS client station. You must also configure Java on the OSS client station by specifying the
location of the truststore file on the OSS client station. For more information, see the TLS
configuration and management information in the NSP Installation and Upgrade Guide .

See 4.12 “To compile and connect an NFM-P JMS client” (p.and 62) the Java documentation for
information about configuring Java to use TLS.

The supported Java version may change between NFM-P releases. A difference in the major or
minor Java version can affect operation, for example:
• TLS 1.2 is the default security mechanism in Java 8.
• In JDK 8u31, the SSLv3 protocol is deactivated.

For details about changes to the Java Runtime Environment, see the Java release notes and
security documentation.

To determine the NFM-P Java version, see4.15 “To determine the Java version” (p. .65)

3.5.2 HTTPS communication with XML API
The XML API can send requests and receive responses using HTTPS, which requires TLS
encryption. See theNSP Planning Guidefor the system requirements associated with TLS and
HTTPS. See theNSP Installation and Upgrade Guide for information about implementing TLS in an
NFM-P system.

3.5.3 Session management
Effective session management requires the AAA functions. Authentication is the verification of a
user identification and password. Authorization is the assignment of different levels of access
permissions to users. Accounting is the recording of user actions. An NFM-P operator can configure
AAA functions using the local security capability of the NFM-P server, a third-party authentication
server, or a combination of local and third-party mechanisms.
• Local authentication on the NFM-P server is provided by a local user database and security
scheme to verify login attempts and assign permission levels for command execution.

OSS user and group management

An NFM-P administrator can use a GUI or OSS client to manage user and group privileges,
sessions, and authentication. Using scope of command and span of control profiles, an
administrator can specify which functions are available to a user or group, and restrict the objects
that users can view or configure. See the section on NFM-P user security NSPin the System
Administrator Guide for more information.

You can configure the following OSS properties of a user account or user group; if the user and
group settings differ, the user settings override the group settings:
• maximum number of allowed OSS sessions per user
• priority assigned to OSS requests
• OSS request timeout

When the number of concurrent sessions reaches the system maximum, the NFM-P uses the
priority values of the outstanding requests to determine which to process next.

Note: After an upgrade, the NFM-P assigns the default priority value to each existing OSS
user and user group.

An OSS request timeout value applies to a request that the NFM-P has accepted but not
processed. If the request processing does not begin before the timeout period elapses, the NFM-P
rejects the request and returns an error.

Client sessions

All client sessions have username and password protection.
• Each OSS client XML/SOAP message is individually authenticated using cached information
from an authorization server.
• JMS messages are protected by the user name and password for the JMS connection.

You can use an MD5-hashed or a clear text password to access the NFM-P server.

MD5-hashed password format

Nokia recommends that you send the password for a request in an MD5-hashed format. You can
use the md5hash password utility to generate MD5-hashed passwords to access the NFM-P server.
See 3.6 “To generate an MD5-hashed password for NFM-P main server access” (p.for 28) more
information about how to generate an MD5-hashed password for NFM-P access.

Note: MD5-hashed passwords do not secure the communication channel.

Note: Nokia recommends enabling TLS for secure communication. See NSPthe Installation
and Upgrade Guidefor TLS configuration and management information.

653→ XML schema changes
654→
655→8.8.1 Overview
656→The XML API has evolved over several releases and expanded and changed with the introduction
657→of various network management and network element functions.
658→
659→8.8.2 Deprecated properties and methods
660→Some deprecated objects of the XML API are subject to change or to be replaced, are no longer in
661→use, or were never supported. Although deprecated objects remain in the software, Nokia
662→recommends that OSS developers not use them because the deprecated object may not be
663→included in a future release.
664→
665→8.8.3 Schema changes for releases
666→The differences between releases of the XML API, including additions, deletions, and changes, are
667→listed at a high level. Changes in the schema can be reviewed by examining details of the interface
668→documentation in each release. Differences can be compared to the methods and objects used in
669→OSS applications to determine whether application updates are required.
670→
671→See 8.10 “To view release-specific XML schema changes” (p. 102)for information about viewing
672→schema changes between releases.
673→
674→Note: If you are planning to use an OSS client that was tested in a previous release of the
675→NFM-P, you must review your usage with the list of schema changes before you start
676→development, in order to identify changes that must be made to the packages, classes, types,
677→methods, or properties that are used by the OSS client.
678→
679→8.8.4 Schema changes for network element versions
680→Various packages, classes, and properties may apply to a subset of network element products and
681→versions. Values and applicability of properties may change after a network element upgrade or
682→downgrade. OSS applications should be designed to process XML API such that extra or missing
683→properties do not cause unexpected OSS behavior. For example, OSS applications should not
684→expect specific assigned values for properties that are not applicable to a particular product version.
685→
686→It is recommended that product-specific differences be compared to the methods and objects used
687→in OSS applications to determine whether application updates are required.
688→
689→See 8.5.14 “Supported network elements” (p. 99)for information about products and releases that
690→support a class. Product-specific details may also apply to various properties.
691→
692→Note: If you are planning to use an OSS client that was tested in a previous release of the
693→NFM-P or are planning to use different network element product versions, you must review
694→your usage with the list of schema changes before you start development in order to identify
695→changes that must be made to the packages, classes, types, methods, or properties that are
696→used by the OSS client.

21→NFM-P GUI
22→− NE-specific properties
23→• relationships between domain objects that indicate the inheritance and containment of these
24→objects

26→definitions specific to NFM-P functions.

237→After you access the XML API Reference, a table appears. The table includes the full package list

247→The information model is a UML drawing that shows the relationships amongst the classes in the
248→selected package and other extended classes from which some properties, methods, and naming
249→are inherited. The classes in the package are represented by white rectangles; the extended
250→classes are represented by gray rectangles. When you click on one of the rectangles, the class
251→information about the selected class is displayed.

253→Most packages have only one information model drawing. However, some of the larger packages
254→(such as service, equipment, and sas) group member classes into separate information models that
255→represent specific functional areas.

258→creation, maintenance, configuration, and testing. As a result, the information model for the
259→package is divided into more than one information model to address the following functional areas:
260→
261→• Access Interface
262→• Operational Group and Encap Group
263→• Connector and Composite Service
264→• STM Service Action
265→• GNE Info
266→• STM Service Ping
267→• Base Service
268→• STM Service Trace
269→• Logical Interface
270→• SAP Policer and Policy Override

273→types that all of the other classes use to inherit from. Perform8.10 “To view release-specific XML

7 XML API information model overview


7.1 XML API information model overview

7.1.1 Overview
The XML API information model maps to the NFM-P Java code base. The model is defined by an
XML schema that is organized in packages.

The information model consists of:
• packages with one or more groups of related domain objects (classes), data types, bitmasks,
and enumerations
• classes that contain:
− properties of the class
− information structures for both the domain objects (classes) and properties of the information,
which are called elements in the XML API but are known as parameters in CLI and the
NFM-P GUI
− NE-specific properties
• relationships between domain objects that indicate the inheritance and containment of these
objects
• standard and specific XML schema definitions of types and methods, as well as XML schema
definitions specific to NFM-P functions.

The information model provides a type of object model of the NFM-P-managed network. The
following figure shows an example of the information model in terms of subscriber configuration.

properties, methods, and supported NE types and releases (right panel)

8.3.1 Overview
After you access the XML API Reference, a table appears. The table includes the full package list
and corresponding descriptions of all of the packages that are available using the XML interface.
Click on a package link in the table for a general description of the package and the information
model diagram.

The package list is also available from the upper left panel of the HTML document. When you
choose All Classes/Structs/Types, or a specific package name from the list of packages, the content
of the class, struct, and types list area in the lower left panel changes. Each package may contain
classes, structs, types, or all.

The information model is a UML drawing that shows the relationships amongst the classes in the
selected package and other extended classes from which some properties, methods, and naming
are inherited. The classes in the package are represented by white rectangles; the extended
classes are represented by gray rectangles. When you click on one of the rectangles, the class
information about the selected class is displayed.

Most packages have only one information model drawing. However, some of the larger packages
(such as service, equipment, and sas) group member classes into separate information models that
represent specific functional areas.

For example, the service package provides specifications for all of the areas that affect service
creation, maintenance, configuration, and testing. As a result, the information model for the
package is divided into more than one information model to address the following functional areas:

• Access Interface
• Operational Group and Encap Group
• Connector and Composite Service
• STM Service Action
• GNE Info
• STM Service Ping
• Base Service
• STM Service Trace
• Logical Interface
• SAP Policer and Policy Override

The $core package, which is a root or base of all of the packages, defines the base classes and
types that all of the other classes use to inherit from. Perform8.10 “To view release-specific XML
schema changes” (p. 102) to view package information in the XML API Reference.

 XML schema changes

8.8.1 Overview
The XML API has evolved over several releases and expanded and changed with the introduction
of various network management and network element functions.

8.8.2 Deprecated properties and methods
Some deprecated objects of the XML API are subject to change or to be replaced, are no longer in
use, or were never supported. Although deprecated objects remain in the software, Nokia
recommends that OSS developers not use them because the deprecated object may not be
included in a future release.

8.8.3 Schema changes for releases
The differences between releases of the XML API, including additions, deletions, and changes, are
listed at a high level. Changes in the schema can be reviewed by examining details of the interface
documentation in each release. Differences can be compared to the methods and objects used in
OSS applications to determine whether application updates are required.

See 8.10 “To view release-specific XML schema changes” (p. 102)for information about viewing
schema changes between releases.

Note: If you are planning to use an OSS client that was tested in a previous release of the
NFM-P, you must review your usage with the list of schema changes before you start
development, in order to identify changes that must be made to the packages, classes, types,
methods, or properties that are used by the OSS client.

8.8.4 Schema changes for network element versions
Various packages, classes, and properties may apply to a subset of network element products and
versions. Values and applicability of properties may change after a network element upgrade or
downgrade. OSS applications should be designed to process XML API such that extra or missing
properties do not cause unexpected OSS behavior. For example, OSS applications should not
expect specific assigned values for properties that are not applicable to a particular product version.

It is recommended that product-specific differences be compared to the methods and objects used
in OSS applications to determine whether application updates are required.

See 8.5.14 “Supported network elements” (p. 99)for information about products and releases that
support a class. Product-specific details may also apply to various properties.

Note: If you are planning to use an OSS client that was tested in a previous release of the
NFM-P or are planning to use different network element product versions, you must review
your usage with the list of schema changes before you start development in order to identify
changes that must be made to the packages, classes, types, methods, or properties that are
used by the OSS client.

575→ Result filtering

577→6.2.1 Overview
578→Result filters limit the attributes, objects, and child objects that are returned in a result. If no attribute
579→tags are defined in a result filter, then all properties at the level of resultFilter are returned. For more
580→information, see the xmlApiTypes.xsd file in the Schema Reference.
581→
582→The <attribute>propertyName</attribute> tag specifies that the property is to be returned. When
583→using multiple levels of nested resultFilter, a single empty attribute tag <attribute/> returns no
584→attributes for that object level.
585→
586→The <children> list of nested resultFilters</children> tag specifies that the given types of children be
587→returned. The nested resultFilters can contain the class attributes specifying the package qualified
588→class name of the child to be returned.
589→
590→If the children tag is empty, no children are returned. If the children tag is not defined, then all
591→children of this object are returned.
592→
593→The class attribute on nested child resultFilters allows a class of ManageObject to be specified,
594→which is the base class for all classes.
595→
596→If the optional recursive attribute is set to yes in the children specification, then the children are
597→filtered according to the same rules as the parent; nested resultFilters are not required or allowed.
598→The recursive attribute default is no. SeeFigure 6-5, “resultFilter example using recursive children
599→attribute” (p. 78)for an example.
600→
601→Within a nested class resultFilter, by specifying an empty <attribute/> tag, no attributes are returned
602→for the specified class object. However, children and grandchildren of that class object can be
603→returned by including attribute tags with values. SeeFigure 6-7, “Nested resultFilter example
604→specifying only child attributes” (p. 79)for an example.

1087→NFM-P GUI
1088→− NE-specific properties
1089→• relationships between domain objects that indicate the inheritance and containment of these
1090→objects
1091→• standard and specific XML schema definitions of types and methods, as well as XML schema

8→5.1 HTTP communication with the NFM-P
9→
10→5.1.1 Overview
11→The XML API is accessible using a servlet that runs on an NFM-P main server. The XML API uses
12→HTTP or HTTPS to transport the XML requests between the client application and the server.
13→
14→To establish communication with the NFM-P, you must develop HTTP client request messages that
15→include the following components:
16→• The address of the NFM-P main server, which is the server hostname or IP address, a colon,
17→and the HTTP or HTTPS TCP port.
18→• A SOAP envelope, which contains one or more XML requests.
19→
20→After the NFM-P executes a request, it returns a response with a status code that indicates the
21→request success or failure, and the information defined in the request.9.1 See “XML message
22→structure ” (p. 105) for information about SOAP request, response, and fault messages.
23→
24→5.2 HTTP POST method
25→
26→5.2.1 Overview
27→The XML API supports only the HTTP POST method for client requests. SOAP messages between
28→the OSS and XML API are transmitted in the HTTP message body. For more information about
29→HTTP, see RFC 2616.
30→

36→including POST that is required to send the XML API requests.
37→You must always close and release the connection regardless of whether the response to your
38→XML request is a success or not. Make sure the connection is not stuck in a CLOSE-WAIT
39→state; use the appropriate HTTP client methods to properly close it.

259→5.7.1 Overview
260→If an OSS application includes an element that is not in the schema in the XML request, the element
261→is ignored and the XML API processes the request. All XML requests with matching start and end
262→tags are accepted by the XML API, including spelling and case errors. The NFM-P logs a message
263→to the serverLogFile.
264→
265→Note: Enabling all logging for the XML API layer is only suitable for development
266→environments.

575→ Result filtering
576→
577→6.2.1 Overview
578→Result filters limit the attributes, objects, and child objects that are returned in a result. If no attribute
579→tags are defined in a result filter, then all properties at the level of resultFilter are returned. For more
580→information, see the xmlApiTypes.xsd file in the Schema Reference.
581→
582→The <attribute>propertyName</attribute> tag specifies that the property is to be returned. When
583→using multiple levels of nested resultFilter, a single empty attribute tag <attribute/> returns no
584→attributes for that object level.
585→
586→The <children> list of nested resultFilters</children> tag specifies that the given types of children be
587→returned. The nested resultFilters can contain the class attributes specifying the package qualified
588→class name of the child to be returned.
589→
590→If the children tag is empty, no children are returned. If the children tag is not defined, then all
591→children of this object are returned.
592→
593→The class attribute on nested child resultFilters allows a class of ManageObject to be specified,
594→which is the base class for all classes.
595→
596→If the optional recursive attribute is set to yes in the children specification, then the children are
597→filtered according to the same rules as the parent; nested resultFilters are not required or allowed.
598→The recursive attribute default is no. SeeFigure 6-5, “resultFilter example using recursive children
599→attribute” (p. 78)for an example.
600→
601→Within a nested class resultFilter, by specifying an empty <attribute/> tag, no attributes are returned
602→for the specified class object. However, children and grandchildren of that class object can be
603→returned by including attribute tags with values. SeeFigure 6-7, “Nested resultFilter example
604→specifying only child attributes” (p. 79)for an example.

5 XML requests


5.1 HTTP communication with the NFM-P

5.1.1 Overview
The XML API is accessible using a servlet that runs on an NFM-P main server. The XML API uses
HTTP or HTTPS to transport the XML requests between the client application and the server.

To establish communication with the NFM-P, you must develop HTTP client request messages that
include the following components:
• The address of the NFM-P main server, which is the server hostname or IP address, a colon,
and the HTTP or HTTPS TCP port.
• A SOAP envelope, which contains one or more XML requests.

After the NFM-P executes a request, it returns a response with a status code that indicates the
request success or failure, and the information defined in the request.9.1 See “XML message
structure ” (p. 105) for information about SOAP request, response, and fault messages.

5.2 HTTP POST method

5.2.1 Overview
The XML API supports only the HTTP POST method for client requests. SOAP messages between
the OSS and XML API are transmitted in the HTTP message body. For more information about
HTTP, see RFC 2616.

5.3 To post an XML request to the NFM-P
Note: You must use a user account with OSS Mgmt permission to access the XML API. See
the chapter on NFM-P user security in the NSP System Administrator Guide for more
information about the NFM-P user accounts and privileges.
You must have an OSS script or application that uses the required HTTP client methods,
including POST that is required to send the XML API requests.
You must always close and release the connection regardless of whether the response to your
XML request is a success or not. Make sure the connection is not stuck in a CLOSE-WAIT
state; use the appropriate HTTP client methods to properly close it.

to the serverLogFile.

environments.

 Result filtering

6.2.1 Overview
Result filters limit the attributes, objects, and child objects that are returned in a result. If no attribute
tags are defined in a result filter, then all properties at the level of resultFilter are returned. For more
information, see the xmlApiTypes.xsd file in the Schema Reference.

The <attribute>propertyName</attribute> tag specifies that the property is to be returned. When
using multiple levels of nested resultFilter, a single empty attribute tag <attribute/> returns no
attributes for that object level.

The <children> list of nested resultFilters</children> tag specifies that the given types of children be
returned. The nested resultFilters can contain the class attributes specifying the package qualified
class name of the child to be returned.

If the children tag is empty, no children are returned. If the children tag is not defined, then all
children of this object are returned.

The class attribute on nested child resultFilters allows a class of ManageObject to be specified,
which is the base class for all classes.

If the optional recursive attribute is set to yes in the children specification, then the children are
filtered according to the same rules as the parent; nested resultFilters are not required or allowed.
The recursive attribute default is no. SeeFigure 6-5, “resultFilter example using recursive children
attribute” (p. 78)for an example.

Within a nested class resultFilter, by specifying an empty <attribute/> tag, no attributes are returned
for the specified class object. However, children and grandchildren of that class object can be
returned by including attribute tags with values. SeeFigure 6-7, “Nested resultFilter example
specifying only child attributes” (p. 79)for an example.

By default, JMS event vessels do not include the JMS header properties of the contained events. In
order to return event header properties, you must specify the properties using the extraTags type
during filter registration. The header properties are then included in the body of each associated
event that has the header property.

If a JMS event does not have a specified header property, the property is excluded from the event
body. If an eventName value is omitted, the specified JMS header property is returned for each
event that has the property.

7.1 XML API information model overview

7.1.1 Overview
The XML API information model maps to the NFM-P Java code base. The model is defined by an
XML schema that is organized in packages.

The information model consists of:
• packages with one or more groups of related domain objects (classes), data types, bitmasks,
and enumerations
• classes that contain:
− properties of the class
− information structures for both the domain objects (classes) and properties of the information,
which are called elements in the XML API but are known as parameters in CLI and the
NFM-P GUI
− NE-specific properties
• relationships between domain objects that indicate the inheritance and containment of these
objects
• standard and specific XML schema definitions of types and methods, as well as XML schema
definitions specific to NFM-P functions.

The information model provides a type of object model of the NFM-P-managed network. The
following figure shows an example of the information model in terms of subscriber configuration.

1045→11.3 Alarm sources
1046→
1047→11.3.1 Overview
1048→The sources that initiate NFM-P alarm notifications are:
1049→• network traps
1050→• NFM-P alarms
1051→
1052→11.3.2 Network traps
1053→The NFM-P monitors network health by listening for traps from the managed network elements.
1054→These SNMP traps may indicate conditions that include configuration or operational state changes,
1055→security breach attempts, and equipment faults.
1056→When the NFM-P detects a fault in the network, one or more alarms are generated, depending on
1057→the cause of the fault. When an alarm is created, modified or deleted the JMS messages that
1058→contain the alarm information are sent to interested listeners.
1059→
1060→Note: Although the NFM-P receives network information in traps and generating alarms about
1061→fault conditions in the network, the traps are not directly mapped to alarms.

1045→11.3 Alarm sources

1047→11.3.1 Overview
1048→The sources that initiate NFM-P alarm notifications are:
1049→• network traps

1051→
1052→11.3.2 Network traps
1053→The NFM-P monitors network health by listening for traps from the managed network elements.
1054→These SNMP traps may indicate conditions that include configuration or operational state changes,
1055→security breach attempts, and equipment faults.
1056→When the NFM-P detects a fault in the network, one or more alarms are generated, depending on
1057→the cause of the fault. When an alarm is created, modified or deleted the JMS messages that
1058→contain the alarm information are sent to interested listeners.
1059→
1060→Note: Although the NFM-P receives network information in traps and generating alarms about
1061→fault conditions in the network, the traps are not directly mapped to alarms.

10 Schema Reference


10.1 Schema Reference

10.1.1 Overview
The Schema Reference describes the structure and allowed elements of an XML document sent to
the NFM-P, such as a configuration or information request. A developer can use the schema to
determine the valid elements, data types, and parameters of an NFM-P functional area, or package.

10.1.2 Package-specific schema files
The following schema files are specific to a package:
• packageMethods.xsd—describes the methods that are available to the package
• packageTypes.xsd—describes the properties of each object, or class, in the package, the
package information structure, and the values assigned to complex types such as bitmask and
enumeration

10.1.3 Viewing the schema of a specific XML package
See the Network Developer Portalto access the Schema Reference. The schema page lists the
method and data type files for each package.

Click on thepackageMethods.xsd or packageTypes.xsd link, as required, where package is the
package of interest. The schema information is displayed.

11 Fault management


11.1 Fault management

11.1.1 Overview
The OSS applications that focus on fault management use events and alarms to detect, log, notify
users of, and automatically correct network problems to keep the network running effectively.

11.2 Communicating with the NFM-P

11.2.1 Overview
An OSS fault management application can use a JMS and/or an XML/SOAP interface to
communicate with the NFM-P server. For alarm management:
• The NFM-P sends network event/alarm notifications using the JMS interface in near-real-time to
the OSS. An OSS uses the JMS event stream to monitor new alarms and status changes on
existing alarms such as clearing or escalation. SeeChapter 4, “Event monitoring using JMS” for
information.

11.3 Alarm sources

11.3.1 Overview
The sources that initiate NFM-P alarm notifications are:
• network traps
• NFM-P alarms

11.3.2 Network traps
The NFM-P monitors network health by listening for traps from the managed network elements.
These SNMP traps may indicate conditions that include configuration or operational state changes,
security breach attempts, and equipment faults.
When the NFM-P detects a fault in the network, one or more alarms are generated, depending on
the cause of the fault. When an alarm is created, modified or deleted the JMS messages that
contain the alarm information are sent to interested listeners.

Note: Although the NFM-P receives network information in traps and generating alarms about
fault conditions in the network, the traps are not directly mapped to alarms.

10→9.1.1 Overview
11→The XML API uses request, response, and fault messages to handle the XML message data related
12→to network objects. Messages are sent to the XML API using an RPC pattern. The messages are
13→constructed and wrapped in a SOAP envelope. The XML API then returns a success response
14→message or a failure fault message.
15→
16→The SOAP encoding transports the XML data. Three types of SOAP messages are used:
17→• requests
18→• responses for a successful or unsuccessful execution
19→• faults for SOAP messages that are not well-formed

9.1 XML message structure

9.1.1 Overview
The XML API uses request, response, and fault messages to handle the XML message data related
to network objects. Messages are sent to the XML API using an RPC pattern. The messages are
constructed and wrapped in a SOAP envelope. The XML API then returns a success response
message or a failure fault message.

The SOAP encoding transports the XML data. Three types of SOAP messages are used:
• requests
• responses for a successful or unsuccessful execution
• faults for SOAP messages that are not well-formed

26→port or channel linked by physical wire, it is the network interface that determines the IP
27→connectivity.

33→• associated L3 interface to a physical port or channel cabled to another device
34→• configured QoS policy. SeeChapter 18, “Policy configuration management” for more information.

90→17.5 Routing protocol configuration
91→
92→17.5.1 Overview
93→A routing protocol specifies how routers communicate with each other, dynamically disseminating
94→information that enables them to select routes between NEs, the choice of the route being done by
95→routing algorithms. The NFM-P supports a variety of standard routing protocols.
96→You can use the XML API to enable and configure network protocol communications and
97→connections on NEs.
98→Supported routing protocols and their packages include:
99→• BGP (bgp)
100→• RIP (rip)
101→• OSPF (ospf)

114→• LDP (ldp)
115→• IS-IS (isis)
116→• L2TP (l2tp)
117→• RSVP (rsvp)
118→
119→The XML API also supports the following multicast protocols:
120→• PIM (pim)
121→• IGMP (igmp)
122→• MSDP (msdp)
123→• MLD (mld)
124→
125→17.5.2 BGP
126→BGP is an inter-AS routing protocol. An AS is a network or a group of devices logically organized
127→and controlled by a common network administration. BGP enables devices to exchange network
128→reachability information. AS paths are the routes to each destination. There are two types of BGP:
129→IBGP and EBGP.
130→• IBGP is used to communicate with peer devices in the same AS.
131→• EBGP is used to communicate with peers in different ASs.
132→
133→17.5.3 RIP
134→RIP is an IGP that uses a distance-vector algorithm to determine the best route to a destination,
135→using hop count as the deciding factor. In order for the protocol to provide complete information
136→about routing, every device in the domain must participate in the protocol. RIP, a UDP-based
137→protocol, updates its neighbors, and the neighbors update their neighbors. RIP directly advertises
138→reachability information to its neighbors by sending prefix, mask, and either hop count or cost metric
139→data.
140→
141→17.5.4 OSPF
142→OSPF is a hierarchical link state protocol. OSPF is an IGP used within large ASs. OSPF routers
143→exchange the state, cost, and other relevant interface information with neighbors after the
144→neighbors are discovered. The information exchange enables all participating routers to establish a
145→network topology map. Each router applies the Dijkstra algorithm to calculate the shortest path to
146→each destination in the network. The resulting OSPF forwarding table is submitted to the routing
147→table manager to calculate the routing table.
148→
149→17.5.5 LDP
150→LDP is used to distribute labels in non-traffic-engineered MPLS applications. Routers can establish
151→LSPs across a network by mapping network-layer routing information directly to the data link layer
152→switched paths. After LDP distributes the labels to the LSR, the LSR assigns the label to a FEC,
153→and then informs all other LSRs in the path about the label and how the label will switch data
154→accordingly.
155→
156→

158→ 
159→           
160→ 2024 1
161→225
162→--- Page 226 ---
163→Network configuration managementRouting protocol configuration
164→
165→
166→17.5.6 IS-IS
167→IS-IS is a link-state IGP that uses the shortest path first algorithm to determine a route. Routing
168→decisions are made using the link-state information. IS-IS entities include:
169→• networks, which are autonomous system routing domains
170→• intermediate systems (supported routers)
171→• end systems, which are network devices that send and receive PDUs
172→
173→End systems and intermediate system protocols allow NEs to identify each other. The IS-IS protocol
174→sends link-state updates periodically through the network, so each NE can maintain current network
175→topology information.
176→
177→17.5.7 L2TP
178→L2PT is a session-layer protocol that extends the PPP model by allowing L2 and PPP endpoints to
179→reside on different devices that are interconnected by a PSN. L2TP extends the PPP sessions
180→between the CPE and PPP/L2TP termination point (LNS), via an intermediate LAC.
181→
182→17.5.8 RSVP
183→RSVP is a network-control protocol in the IP suite that is used for communicating application QoS
184→requirements to intermediate transit NEs in a network. RSVP uses a soft-state mechanism to
185→maintain path and reservation states on each NE in the reservation path.
186→
187→17.5.9 PIM
188→PIM is a multicast routing architecture that allows the addition of IP multicast routing on existing IP
189→networks. PIM is unicast routing protocol independent and can be operated in the following ways:
190→• sparse mode
191→• dense mode
192→
193→17.5.10 IGMP
194→The XML API uses the igmp package to configure the multicast IGMP routing type on IPv4 hosts
195→and routers. IPv4 hosts and routers use IGMP to report their group memberships to neighboring
196→multicast routers.
197→
198→17.5.11 MSDP
199→MSDP is a protocol that enables multiple PIM-SM domains to communicate with each other using
200→their own RPs. MSDP also enables multiple RPs in a single PIM-SM domain to establish MSDP
201→mesh-groups and to synchronize information between anycast RPs about the active sources being
202→served by each anycast RP peer.
203→
204→17.5.12 MLD
205→MLD is an asymmetric protocol used by IPv6 routers to discover the presence of NEs that wish to
206→receive multicast packets on their directly-attached links, and to discover which multicast addresses
207→are of interest to those neighboring NEs.

17.5.8 RSVP
RSVP is a network-control protocol in the IP suite that is used for communicating application QoS
requirements to intermediate transit NEs in a network. RSVP uses a soft-state mechanism to
maintain path and reservation states on each NE in the reservation path.

17.5.9 PIM
PIM is a multicast routing architecture that allows the addition of IP multicast routing on existing IP
networks. PIM is unicast routing protocol independent and can be operated in the following ways:
• sparse mode
• dense mode

17.5.10 IGMP
The XML API uses the igmp package to configure the multicast IGMP routing type on IPv4 hosts
and routers. IPv4 hosts and routers use IGMP to report their group memberships to neighboring
multicast routers.

17.5.11 MSDP
MSDP is a protocol that enables multiple PIM-SM domains to communicate with each other using
their own RPs. MSDP also enables multiple RPs in a single PIM-SM domain to establish MSDP
mesh-groups and to synchronize information between anycast RPs about the active sources being
served by each anycast RP peer.

17.5.12 MLD
MLD is an asymmetric protocol used by IPv6 routers to discover the presence of NEs that wish to
receive multicast packets on their directly-attached links, and to discover which multicast addresses
are of interest to those neighboring NEs.

17.9.3 LSP
An LSP is a path through an MPLS network that is set up based on criteria in a forwarding
equivalency class, or FEC. LSPs are unidirectional; they enable the label switching of a packet
through an MPLS network from one endpoint to another. Bidirectional communication through an
MPLS network requires the configuration of an LSP in the opposite direction.

17.9.4 Service tunnels
A service tunnel is an entity used to uni-directionally direct traffic from one device to another device.
The service tunnel is provisioned to use a specific encapsulation method, such as GRE or MPLS,
and the services are then mapped to the service tunnel. The most common type of tunnel used in
the NFM-P is a service distribution point binding. Service tunnels originate on an SDP on a source
NE and terminate at a destination NE.

Note: See “MPLS” and “Service tunnels” in the NSP NFM-P Classic Management User Guide
for more information about MPLS, LSPs, and service tunnels.

782→15.3.5 Deployment failure recovery procedures
783→The deployment failure recovery procedures to be carried out varies with the type of action
784→(creation, modification, or deletion):
785→• If deployment fails during object creation, you must clear the deployments to remove the
786→previously created object from the database. To remove the possibility of partially-created
787→objects on an NE, resynchronize the object (this can be done using the
788→generic.GenericObject.triggerResync method) and remove all partially-created objects using the
789→XML API or the NFM-P.
790→• If deployment fails during object modification, clearing a deployment does not reset the modified
791→object in the database. To reset to the previous object setting, resynchronize the object. In there
792→are partially-modified objects, set the objects back to their original values using the XML API or
793→the NFM-P.
794→• If deployment fails during object deletion, clearing a deployment completes the object deletion in
795→the NFM-P database. To reset to the previous object setting, resynchronize the object.
796→
797→See 15.4 “Workflow to handle deployment failures” (p. 216)in this chapter for more information
798→about handling a deployment error that has caused the NFM-P database to be out of
799→synchronization with the managed network.

10→15.1.1 Overview
11→OSS applications can use the XML API to perform configuration operations on NFM-P-managed
12→network objects and their associated child objects. This is achieved by sending XML requests that
13→allow the OSS to create, delete, or modify existing objects. These requests can also extend to the
14→object’s children at the same time, if required.

16→Note: The configuration operations that are allowed on each object is defined in the XML
17→schema. See the Schema Reference. See the XML API Reference for more information about
18→the object hierarchies (relationship between parent and child objects).
19→
20→The OSS user account privileges define the access and restrictions for configuration operations in
21→NFM-P functional areas. See the chapter on NFM-P user security in NSP the System Administrator
22→Guide for information about configuring user accounts and assigning privileges.
23→
24→Most of the configuration operations that can be performed on the functional areas of the NFM-P
25→using the GUI can also be performed using the XML API. The main areas for OSS configuration
26→management include:
27→• device configuration—for example, routers, cards, ports, GNE, and channels. ChapterSee 16,
28→“Device configuration management”for more information.
29→• network configuration—for example, protocols, MPLS, service tunnels, and VRRP. ChapterSee
30→17, “Network configuration management” for more information.
31→• policy configuration—for example, service policy, routing policy, and network policy.Chapter See
32→18, “Policy configuration management” for more information.
33→• service configuration—for example, VLL, VPLS, VPRN, VLAN, mirror composite, and customer/
34→subscriber. See Chapter 19, “Service configuration management” for more information.
35→• scripts and template configuration—See Chapter 20, “Script and template configuration
36→management” for more information.

782→15.3.5 Deployment failure recovery procedures
783→The deployment failure recovery procedures to be carried out varies with the type of action
784→(creation, modification, or deletion):
785→• If deployment fails during object creation, you must clear the deployments to remove the
786→previously created object from the database. To remove the possibility of partially-created
787→objects on an NE, resynchronize the object (this can be done using the
788→generic.GenericObject.triggerResync method) and remove all partially-created objects using the
789→XML API or the NFM-P.
790→• If deployment fails during object modification, clearing a deployment does not reset the modified
791→object in the database. To reset to the previous object setting, resynchronize the object. In there
792→are partially-modified objects, set the objects back to their original values using the XML API or
793→the NFM-P.
794→• If deployment fails during object deletion, clearing a deployment completes the object deletion in
795→the NFM-P database. To reset to the previous object setting, resynchronize the object.
796→
797→See 15.4 “Workflow to handle deployment failures” (p. 216)in this chapter for more information
798→about handling a deployment error that has caused the NFM-P database to be out of
799→synchronization with the managed network.
800→
801→15.3.6 Deployment alarms and events
802→OSS applications that rely on alarms and events to notify them of deployment failures must
803→subscribe to the JMS interface. SeeChapter 4, “Event monitoring using JMS” for information.
804→
805→The DeployerEvent indicates the success or failure of an asynchronous deployment request and
806→will return a successList and failedList of deployerIds. SeeFigure B-7, “DeployerEvent message
807→example” (p. 343)for a DeployerEvent message example. An OSS can then take the failed
808→deployerId and retrieve more information on the reason for the failure and then perform the required
809→recovery procedure.
810→
811→Deployment alarms are also raised and OSS applications can use the requestId and the
812→requestUser to match failures with specific requests. After the deployerId is extracted from the
813→alarm, you can use the deployerId to query a specific deployment. See the XML API SDK Sample
814→Code Navigator for a sample request to retrieve deployment information.
815→
816→Figure 15-12, “Deployment alarm example” (p. 214)shows a deployment alarm example. The
817→following information is contained in the deployment alarm:

15 Configuration management overview


15.1 Configuration management

15.1.1 Overview
OSS applications can use the XML API to perform configuration operations on NFM-P-managed
network objects and their associated child objects. This is achieved by sending XML requests that
allow the OSS to create, delete, or modify existing objects. These requests can also extend to the
object’s children at the same time, if required.

Note: The configuration operations that are allowed on each object is defined in the XML
schema. See the Schema Reference. See the XML API Reference for more information about
the object hierarchies (relationship between parent and child objects).

The OSS user account privileges define the access and restrictions for configuration operations in
NFM-P functional areas. See the chapter on NFM-P user security in NSP the System Administrator
Guide for information about configuring user accounts and assigning privileges.

Most of the configuration operations that can be performed on the functional areas of the NFM-P
using the GUI can also be performed using the XML API. The main areas for OSS configuration
management include:
• device configuration—for example, routers, cards, ports, GNE, and channels. ChapterSee 16,
“Device configuration management”for more information.
• network configuration—for example, protocols, MPLS, service tunnels, and VRRP. ChapterSee
17, “Network configuration management” for more information.
• policy configuration—for example, service policy, routing policy, and network policy.Chapter See
18, “Policy configuration management” for more information.
• service configuration—for example, VLL, VPLS, VPRN, VLAN, mirror composite, and customer/
subscriber. See Chapter 19, “Service configuration management” for more information.
• scripts and template configuration—See Chapter 20, “Script and template configuration
management” for more information.

15.3.3 Synchronous and asynchronous requests
You can configure the following deployment types:
• asynchronous (default)
• synchronous

Synchronous requests

Users can specify synchronous network requests using the <synchronousDeploy> and other tags.
These requests are sent by the OSS to the NFM-P server where the request is validated and then


<SOAP:Body>


saved to the NFM-P database. Subsequently, a deployment is created and queued on the NFM-P
server for dispatching to the network. When the deployment has successfully performed the
deployment across the network, or when all of the retries specified in the request are completed,
the synchronous response is returned and the deployment put back in the pool of available
deployments. There may be cases where a deployment causes some objects to be resynchronized
from the NE. In these cases, the response is deferred until after the resynchronization has
completed.

If there is a failure of all retries, an alarm is raised that contains details of the failed deployment and
a failure XML response is sent back containing the failed deployment Id.Figure See 9-2, “Database
interaction with synchronous network deployment” (p. 107)for a synchronous network deployment.

15.3.5 Deployment failure recovery procedures
The deployment failure recovery procedures to be carried out varies with the type of action
(creation, modification, or deletion):
• If deployment fails during object creation, you must clear the deployments to remove the
previously created object from the database. To remove the possibility of partially-created
objects on an NE, resynchronize the object (this can be done using the
generic.GenericObject.triggerResync method) and remove all partially-created objects using the
XML API or the NFM-P.
• If deployment fails during object modification, clearing a deployment does not reset the modified
object in the database. To reset to the previous object setting, resynchronize the object. In there
are partially-modified objects, set the objects back to their original values using the XML API or
the NFM-P.
• If deployment fails during object deletion, clearing a deployment completes the object deletion in
the NFM-P database. To reset to the previous object setting, resynchronize the object.

See 15.4 “Workflow to handle deployment failures” (p. 216)in this chapter for more information
about handling a deployment error that has caused the NFM-P database to be out of
synchronization with the managed network.

15.3.6 Deployment alarms and events
OSS applications that rely on alarms and events to notify them of deployment failures must
subscribe to the JMS interface. SeeChapter 4, “Event monitoring using JMS” for information.

The DeployerEvent indicates the success or failure of an asynchronous deployment request and
will return a successList and failedList of deployerIds. SeeFigure B-7, “DeployerEvent message
example” (p. 343)for a DeployerEvent message example. An OSS can then take the failed
deployerId and retrieve more information on the reason for the failure and then perform the required
recovery procedure.

Deployment alarms are also raised and OSS applications can use the requestId and the
requestUser to match failures with specific requests. After the deployerId is extracted from the
alarm, you can use the deployerId to query a specific deployment. See the XML API SDK Sample
Code Navigator for a sample request to retrieve deployment information.

Figure 15-12, “Deployment alarm example” (p. 214)shows a deployment alarm example. The

content.text: I have a comprehensive understanding of the XML API Developer Guide. The user asked me to analyze it as a reference. I'll write a clear Spanish analysis that:

Sí, leí el **XML API Developer Guide 24.11** (`3HE-20022-AAAC-TQZZA`). Es la pieza que faltaba: define **cómo un OSS (nuestro shell) habla con el NFM-P**, no cómo se ve la GUI.

## Qué es el XML API

Hay **dos canales**, no uno:

| Canal | Protocolo | Dirección | Para qué |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Request/response** | SOAP XML sobre HTTP(S) `POST /xmlapi/invoke` | bidireccional | inventory, provisionar, ack alarmas |
| **Eventos** | **JMS** (tópicos `5620-SAM-topic-xml-*`) | NFM-P → cliente | alarmas, ObjectCreation, AttributeValueChange, DeployerEvent |

También existe **NSP REST + Kafka**; esta guía se centra en XML/JMS. El cliente puede ser un CLI (exactamente lo que estamos haciendo).

Auth en **cada** SOAP header:

```xml
<security>
  <user>admin</user>
  <password hashed="false">Nokia1234!</password>
</security>
<requestID>nsp-grok@1</requestID>
```

Hace falta rol **OSS Management**. Span of control se aplica en HTTP; en JMS hay que filtrar a mano (`ALA_span like '%:2:%'`).

## Modelo de objetos (lo que importa para el shell)

Todo es `paquete.Clase` + **FDN** (`objectFullName`). El `$core` es la raíz.

| Dominio | Paquetes | Clases típicas |
|---|---|---|
| Equipment | `netw`, `equipment` | `netw.NetworkElement`, `equipment.PhysicalPort`, `equipment.CardSlot` |
| Routing | `rtr`, `ospf`, `isis`, `ldp`, `rsvp`, `bgp` | `rtr.VirtualRouter`, `rtr.NetworkInterface` |
| MPLS | `mpls` | `mpls.Site`, `mpls.Interface`, `mpls.DynamicLSP`, `mpls.ProvisionedPath` |
| Túneles | `svt` | SDP / service tunnel |
| Servicios | `service`, `vprn`, `vpls`, `vll`/`epipe`, `ies`, `subscr` | `svc-mgr:service-ID` |
| Fallos | `fm` | `fm.AlarmObject`, `fm.FaultManager` |
| Stats | `statistics`, `log` | MIB log records |
| Genérico | `generic` | `generic.GenericObject` (CRUD de todo) |

### FDNs reales (Table 10-4)

Hoy el lab usa atajos (`ne:PE-BAIRES-01`). En NFM-P 24.11 son así:

```
network:10.10.1.1
network:10.10.1.1:shelf-1:cardSlot-1:card:daughterCardSlot-1:daughterCard:port-1
network:10.10.1.1:router-1
network:10.10.1.1:router-1:mpls
network:10.10.1.1:router-1:mpls:interface-1
lsp:from-10.10.1.1-id-1
lsp:from-10.10.1.1-id-1:lsppath-2
provisionedMplsTePath:from-10.10.1.1-id-1
svc-mgr:service-100
svc-mgr:service-100:10.10.1.1
subscriber:12
faultManager:network@10.10.1.1@...|alarm-...
```

Nokia recomienda **nunca hardcodear FDNs**: hacer `find` y usar el `objectFullName` que devuelve.

## Métodos que el CLI debería mapear

**Lectura (inventory)**

```xml
<find xmlns="xmlapi_1.0">
  <fullClassName>netw.NetworkElement</fullClassName>
  <filter><equal name="siteId" value="10.10.1.1"/></filter>
  <resultFilter>
    <attribute>objectFullName</attribute>
    <attribute>displayedName</attribute>
    <children recursive="yes"/>
  </resultFilter>
</find>
```

- `find` → `ls` / `show` / `/ne`
- `findToFile` → exports grandes
- `fm.FaultManager.findFaults` → `/alarms`
- `ping` / `version` / `timeStamp` → `/status`

**Escritura (siempre `generic.GenericObject`)**

| Operación | Método | Equivalente en el shell |
|---|---|---|
| modificar | `configureInstanceWithResult` | `show` + edit, `mpls lsp shutdown` |
| crear hijo | `configureChildInstanceWithResult` | `mpls lsp create`, crear Epipe |
| borrar | `deleteInstance` | `mpls lsp delete` |
| CLI al NE | `netw.NetworkElement.executeCli` | sesión CLI (User Guide cap. 10) |

`actionMask`: `create` / `modify` / `delete`. Deploy: `immediate`, sync o async. Si el deploy falla → `generic.DeploymentFailure` + hay que `clearDeployer` y `triggerResync`.

**Alarmas**

- JMS `ObjectCreation` / `AttributeValueChange` con `fm.AlarmInfo`
- Ack/clear: `fm.FaultManager` (`acknowledgeFault`, `clearFaultsOnObject`)

## Workflow MPLS (cap. 17.10) — el que nos importa

Asume IGP ya up en system interface:

1. Enable MPLS en el router + L3 interfaces → `mpls.Site`
2. Asignar network interface a la instancia MPLS → `mpls.Interface`
3. Mesh de **provisioned paths** → `mpls.ProvisionedPath`
4. Mesh de **LSPs** bound a esos paths → `mpls.DynamicLSP` (unidireccional: hay que crear el inverso)
5. **Service tunnels** en ambos sentidos (`svt`) — GRE o MPLS LSP

Después recién vienen VPRN/VPLS/Epipe (cap. 19): customer → service → site → SAP → SDP binding.

## Cómo encaja con NSP-Grok

El shell ya imita esas operaciones; el API dice **el contrato real**:

| Comando actual | Debería terminar siendo |
|---|---|
| `ls` / `cd` / `show` | `find` + `resultFilter` sobre FDN |
| `/ne` | `find` `netw.NetworkElement` |
| `/mpls lsps` | `find` `mpls.DynamicLSP` |
| `mpls lsp create` | `configureChildInstanceWithResult` bajo `network:IP:router-1:mpls` |
| `mpls lsp shutdown` | `configureInstanceWithResult` `administrativeState` |
| `/alarms` + `ack` | `findFaults` + `fm.FaultManager.acknowledgeFault` |
| `/resync` | `generic.GenericObject.triggerResync` |
| `/status` | `ping` + `version` |
| (nuevo) `cli <ne> "..."` | `netw.NetworkElement.executeCli` |

Hoy el lab es in-memory. El siguiente paso natural, con esta guía, es una capa `xmlapi` que arme SOAP, hable con `/xmlapi/invoke`, y deje los mismos comandos.

No toqué código todavía: lo dejaste como referencia. Si querés, el siguiente movimiento es alinear FDNs/clases en el lab y dejar un backend `mock | xmlapi` para cuando tengas un NFM-P real.

import json

p = r"C:\Users\elzoy\OneDrive\Documents\Code\nsp-2411-api\nsp-2411-api\data\nsp-catalog.json"
with open(p, encoding="utf-8") as f:
    data = json.load(f)

want = {
    "authentication",
    "location",
    "samo_managed objects",
    "samo_generic",
    "samo_general",
    "samo_netw",
    "samo_equipment",
    "samo_mpls",
    "samo_mplstp",
    "samo_svt",
    "samo_ldp",
    "samo_rsvp",

    "samo_service",
    "samo_vprn",
    "samo_vpls",
    "samo_epipe",
    "samo_vll",
    "samo_fm",
    "samo_statistics",
    "samo_topology",
    "alarms",
    "alarmedObjects",
    "networkElements",
    "ports",
    "nsp-services",
}

by = {s["service"]: s for s in data}
for name in sorted(want):
    s = by.get(name)
    if not s:

    print(f"desc={s.get('description')}")
    for e in s.get("endpoints", []):
        print(f"  {e.get('method'):6} {e.get('path')}")

content.text: Good. Write a thorough but readable analysis.

Sí, leí el catálogo. No es un Swagger OpenAPI completo: es el inventario que sale de `GET /v1/location/services` de tu NSP vivo. 209 servicios, 1821 endpoints.

El sistema real es **dos backends**, no uno.

| Host | Qué es | Auth |
|---|---|---|
| `https://172.24.80.28:443` | NSP (REST Gateway, Fault Mgmt, Network/Service Supervision) | OAuth2 `POST /v1/auth/token` |
| `https://172.24.80.21:8443/nfm-p/rest/api` | **NFM-P REST** (`samo_*`) | mismo token NSP, o user/pass estilo XML API |

`samo_*` es el XML API de la guía, expuesto como REST. Los nombres de paquete coinciden: `mpls`, `svt`, `fm`, `netw`, `equipment`, `rtr`, `service`.

## Tres capas para el mismo objeto

Para un LSP o un NE hay **tres APIs distintas**. Conviene no mezclarlas:

**1. Lectura rápida (NSP Supervision)** — GET, FDN, árbol

```
GET  /NetworkSupervision/rest/api/v1/networkElements
GET  /NetworkSupervision/rest/api/v1/networkElements/{fdn}/shelves/{shelf}/cards/{card}/ports
GET  /ServiceSupervision/rest/api/v1/nspServices/lsps
GET  /ServiceSupervision/rest/api/v1/nspServices/services
GET  /ServiceSupervision/rest/api/v1/nspServices/tunnels
GET  /FaultManagement/rest/api/v2/alarms
POST /FaultManagement/rest/api/v2/alarms/{alarmFdn}/acknowledgements
```

Esto es lo más parecido a `ls` / `cd` / `show` / `/alarms`.

**2. CRUD genérico NFM-P (el motor)** — cualquier clase, por FDN

```
GET/PUT/DELETE  /nfm-p/rest/api/v1/managedobjects/{fdn}
POST            /nfm-p/rest/api/v1/managedobjects/search
POST            /nfm-p/rest/api/v1/managedobjects/{fdn}/children

POST /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/generic/GenericObject/configureInstanceWithResult
POST /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/generic/GenericObject/configureChildInstanceWithResult
DELETE /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/generic/GenericObject/deleteInstance
POST /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/generic/GenericObject/triggerResync
POST /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/general/find
POST /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/general/ping
GET  /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/general/version
```

Esto es exactamente el cap. 10 y 15 de la guía XML, en REST.

**3. Acciones de dominio NFM-P** — métodos específicos (reboot, turnUp, findRsvpSessions…)

No listan el objeto: **hacen** algo sobre un `instanceFullName` (el FDN).

## Mapeo al shell

| Comando NSP-Grok | API viva que le corresponde |
|---|---|
| login | `POST /rest-gateway/rest/api/v1/auth/token` |
| `/status` | `POST .../general/ping` + `GET .../general/version` |
| `ls` / `find` / `show` | `POST .../general/find` o `POST .../managedobjects/search` |
| `cd equipment/...` | `GET /v1/networkElements/{fdn}/shelves/.../ports` |
| `/ne` | `GET /v1/networkElements` **o** `find` `netw.NetworkElement` |
| `/resync` | `POST .../netw/NetworkElement/fullResync/{fdn}` |
| CLI al NE | `PUT .../netw/NetworkElement/executeCli/{fdn}` |
| `/mpls lsps` | `GET /v1/nspServices/lsps` **o** `find` `mpls.DynamicLsp` |
| `mpls lsp show` | `GET .../managedobjects/{lspFdn}` + `POST .../mpls/Lsp/findServices/{fdn}` |
| `mpls lsp create` | `POST .../generic/GenericObject/configureChildInstanceWithResult` (clase `mpls.DynamicLsp`) |
| `mpls lsp shutdown` | no hay `Lsp/shutDown`; se hace **modify** de `administrativeState` vía generic, o `svt/AbstractTunnel/shutDown` para SDP |
| `/services` | `GET /v1/nspServices/services` |
| `service turnup` | `POST .../service/Service/turnUp/{fdn}` |
| `/alarms` | `GET /FaultManagement/rest/api/v2/alarms` (NSP) **o** `POST .../fm/FaultManager/findFaults` |
| `alarm ack` | `POST /v2/alarms/{fdn}/acknowledgements` **o** `POST .../fm/FaultManager/acknowledgeFault` |
| `/topology` | `samo_topology` (CPAM: SPF, IGP, checkpoints) — no es un mapa ASCII |

## MPLS en tu sistema (`samo_mpls`, 35 endpoints)

Casi todo es **acción sobre instancia**, no listado:

- Config: `Site/configure`, `Interface/configure`, `Tunnel/configure`, `Tunnel/configureTunnelAndPath`, `Crossconnect/configure`
- Relaciones: `Lsp/findServices`, `DynamicLsp/findRsvpSessions`, `DynamicLsp/findCrossconnects`, `Tunnel/findActualPath` / `findProvisionedPath`
- Extra: path optimization, P2MP, SRLG, hops

Listar LSPs **no** está en `samo_mpls`. Se hace con:

- `POST /v2/general/find` + `fullClassName: mpls.DynamicLsp`
- o `GET /v1/nspServices/lsps` (Supervision)

SDP: `samo_svt` sí tiene `AbstractTunnel/turnUp|shutDown`.  
RSVP/LDP: `samo_rsvp`, `samo_ldp` (configure site/interface, find sessions).  
MPLS-TP: `samo_mplstp` (create with autofill).

## Lectura vs escritura (regla práctica)

Para el CLI:

- **Navegar / listar / alarmas / servicios / LSPs** → APIs NSP en `:443` (GET, más simples).
- **Crear / modificar / shutdown / resync / CLI al NE** → NFM-P `samo_*` en `:8443`, sobre todo `managedobjects` + `generic`.

Auth unificado: un token OAuth2 del REST Gateway y se reusa en ambos hosts.

## Qué no está en este JSON

Es un **catálogo de paths**, no los bodies. Faltan schemas de request (`fullClassName`, `filter`, `configInfo`, `actionMask`, FDN). Eso sigue viviendo en la guía XML + XML API Reference.

Cuando quieras, el siguiente paso concreto es un backend `nsp` en el shell: login contra `172.24.80.28`, `ls`/`show` contra Supervision + `find`, y writes contra `generic`/`managedobjects`.

content.text: There's already an nsp-2411-api project with customer, service, browse CLI! The user might want me to enhance nsp-grok-2411 based on this, or they want the grok shell to do customer→service navigation...
En el otro repo ya hay CLI de customer/servicio. Lo cruzo con la guía de Service Management y rearmo la navegación en este shell.

1→"""``nsp customers``: navegador interactivo de clientes (``subscr.Subscriber``) y sus
servicios VPRN/VPLS/Epipe -- pedido explícito (2026-09-04/05): NFM-P organiza los
servicios por cliente antes que por tipo, y el usuario quiere navegar así en vez de
por la lista plana de `nsp service`.

**Primer comando de esta CLI con nombre en plural** -- pedido explícito del usuario
("nsp customers", no "nsp customer"); queda pendiente, sin hacer todavía, renombrar
el resto de los comandos (`service`, `alarm`, etc.) a plural para ser consistentes --
tarea aparte, no parte de este cambio.
10→
Mismo criterio que `nsp bgp`: **no reusa `domain/inventory.py`** (ese motor es
REST/HATEOAS; esto es SAM-O v3 puro, vía `domain/customerview.py`) -- reusa sólo el
picker de `cli/browse.py`, el mismo mecanismo que ya usan las acciones VPRN/VPLS de
`cli/service.py`. Los helpers chicos (`_session`/`_output`/`_pause_before_menu`/
`_read_prompt`) están duplicados a propósito, no importados de `cli/service.py` --
mismo criterio ya establecido en todo el resto de esta CLI (`kpi.py`/`wf.py`/`bgp.py`/
`ne.py`/`alarm.py`/`service.py` duplican los mismos helpers cada uno, un archivo por
comando, no acoplados entre sí).

20→**Navegación de 4 niveles**: cliente -> tipo de servicio (sólo los que tiene, pedido
explícito: "si tiene: VPRN, VPLS y EPIPE") -> servicio de ese tipo -> detalle +
acciones. Mismo criterio de cancelación por nivel que `cli/service.py._browse_children()`:
Esc/q en el nivel más profundo vuelve un nivel, no todos, hasta llegar arriba de todo.

**Detalle VPRN/VPLS converge con `domain/vpnview.py`/`domain/bgpview.py`, no los
duplica.** Acá ya tenemos el `service_id` (atributo `id` de `vprn.Vprn`/`vpls.Vpls`,
confirmado por el usuario) sin pasar por la superficie REST de `nsp service` -- las
acciones llaman las mismas funciones de dominio que ya usa `cli/service.py`
(`locate_vprn_prefix`, `retrieve_vrf_routes`, `vpls_topology`, `locate_vpls_mac`), más
30→`static-routes`/`bgp-peers` (ver `domain/vpnview.py.find_static_routes()`/
`domain/bgpview.py.find_bgp_peers_for_service()`, ambas confirmadas reales 2026-09-05)
y `overlay` (route-target -> next-hops -> cruce contra los sites de esta VPRN, ver
`_vprn_detail_options()`) -- sin necesitar `_prepare_vpn_action()` (esa función
resuelve `service_id` a partir de un `fdn` REST; acá ya lo tenemos directo del `find`
de SAM-O)."""
from __future__ import annotations

import sys
from typing import Any, Callable
40→
import typer

from . import _command, _global, browse
from ._typer_ext import default_group
from .ne_cli import CONTEXT as NFMP_V3_CONTEXT
from ..catalog import resolver
from ..config import profiles
from ..core.session import Session
from ..domain import bgpview, customerview, samov3, vpnview
50→from ..render import table as render_table

customer_app = typer.Typer(
    cls=default_group("browse"),
    help="Navegador interactivo de clientes (subscr.Subscriber) y sus servicios VPRN/VPLS/Epipe.",
)

# Confirmadas por el usuario (Postman/documentación propia) -- ver
# domain/customerview.py.
SUBSCRIBER_COLUMNS = ["displayedName", "subscriberId"]
60→SERVICE_COLUMNS = ["displayedName", "id", "serviceId", "administrativeState", "operationalState"]
_ROUTES_SITE_COLUMNS = ["displayedName", "siteId", "administrativeState", "operationalState"]

# Mismo `PAGE_SIZE` que el resto de los navegadores (ne.py/service.py/alarm.py) --
# ver `browse.paged()` sobre por qué no alcanza con `page_size=len(lista)` para
# "mostrarla toda en una sola página" en una lista que puede ser larga (clientes,
# servicios de un cliente grande).
_PAGE_SIZE = 25


70→# Ver cli/_command.py -- helpers de comando compartidos (Tier 1 del reorg de
# arquitectura, 2026-09-05).
_session = _command.build_session
_output = _command.render
_field = _command.field
_pause_before_menu = _command.pause_before_menu
_read_prompt = _command.read_prompt


def _base(session: Session) -> str:
80→    return _command.base_for(session, NFMP_V3_CONTEXT, lambda: resolver.resolve(samov3.REQUEST_PATH).base_url)


def _show_subscriber_summary(row: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    display = {col: _field(row, col) for col in SUBSCRIBER_COLUMNS}
    render_table.render([display], columns=SUBSCRIBER_COLUMNS)


def _show_service_summary(row: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    display = {col: _field(row, col) for col in SERVICE_COLUMNS}
90→    render_table.render([display], columns=SERVICE_COLUMNS)


def _vprn_detail_options(session: Session, base: str, service_id: str) -> dict[str, Callable[[], None]]:
    """Acciones de detalle para un VPRN puntual -- las dos que ya existían en
    `cli/service.py` (`locate-prefix`/`routes`), dos de la vuelta anterior
    (`static-routes`/`bgp-peers`), y `overlay` -- nueva, agregada 2026-09-05 a
    partir del flujo real que el usuario confirmó a mano contra CPAM/CPAA: un
    route-target -> `bgpview.find_route_target_next_hops()` (los PEs que lo
    anuncian) -> cada uno cruzado contra `vpnview.find_vprn_site()` para saber
100→    si ese PE es un site de *esta* VPRN puntual y su `operationalState`."""

    def _locate_prefix() -> None:
        prefix = _read_prompt("Prefijo a buscar (ej. 10.0.0.0/24)")
        if prefix is None:
            _pause_before_menu()
            return
        matches = vpnview.locate_vprn_prefix(session, base, service_id, prefix)
        if not matches:
            typer.echo("Sin resultados -- puede ser que el prefijo no esté configurado en ningún SAP.", err=True)
110→        else:
            _output(matches)
        _pause_before_menu()

    def _routes() -> None:
        sites = vpnview.find_vprn_sites(session, base, service_id)
        if not sites:
            typer.echo("No encontré sites para este servicio.", err=True)
            _pause_before_menu()
            return
120→        site = browse.pick(
            browse.paged(sites, _PAGE_SIZE),
            _ROUTES_SITE_COLUMNS,
            _PAGE_SIZE,
            title=f"svc-mgr:service-{service_id} -- elegí un nodo",
        )
        if site is None:
            return  # cancelado desde el picker de nodos -- directo al menú, sin pausa
        site_dn = site.get("objectFullName")
        if not site_dn:
130→            typer.echo("No encontré el DN de ese site -- no puedo pedir sus rutas.", err=True)
            _pause_before_menu()
            return
        subnet = _read_prompt("Subnet a consultar (ej. 10.0.0.0/24)")
        if subnet is None:
            _pause_before_menu()
            return
        try:
            routes = vpnview.retrieve_vrf_routes(session, base, service_id, site_dn, subnet)
        except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 - se muestra el error, no puede tirar el menú
140→            typer.echo(f"Error consultando rutas VRF: {exc}", err=True)
            _pause_before_menu()
            return
        _output(routes)
        _pause_before_menu()

    def _static_routes() -> None:
        try:
            routes = vpnview.find_static_routes(session, base, service_id)
        except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 - se muestra el error, no puede tirar el menú
150→            typer.echo(f"Error consultando rutas estáticas: {exc}", err=True)
            _pause_before_menu()
            return
        if not routes:
            typer.echo("Sin rutas estáticas configuradas en esta VPRN.", err=True)
        else:
            _output(routes)
        _pause_before_menu()

    def _bgp_peers() -> None:
160→        try:
            peers = bgpview.find_bgp_peers_for_service(session, base, service_id)
        except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 - se muestra el error, no puede tirar el menú
            typer.echo(f"Error consultando peers BGP: {exc}", err=True)
            _pause_before_menu()
            return
        if not peers:
            typer.echo("Sin peers BGP para esta VPRN (o BGP no está configurado acá).", err=True)
        else:
            _output(peers)
170→        _pause_before_menu()

    def _overlay() -> None:
        rt = _read_prompt("Route-target a buscar (ej. 65000:10)")
        if rt is None:
            _pause_before_menu()
            return
        try:
            next_hops = bgpview.find_route_target_next_hops(session, base, rt)
        except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 - se muestra el error, no puede tirar el menú
180→            typer.echo(f"Error consultando el overlay BGP: {exc}", err=True)
            _pause_before_menu()
            return
        if not next_hops:
            typer.echo(
                "Sin next-hops para ese route-target (¿no hay overlay CPAM/CPAA para este RT?).", err=True
            )
            _pause_before_menu()
            return
        rows = []
190→        for nh in next_hops:
            pe_ip = nh.get("nextHop")
            site = vpnview.find_vprn_site(session, base, service_id, pe_ip) if pe_ip else None
            rows.append(
                {
                    "nextHop": pe_ip,
                    "esSiteDeEstaVPRN": site is not None,
                    "operationalState": site.get("operationalState") if site else "",
                }
            )
200→        _output(rows)

120→    """Servicios Epipe (``epipe.Epipe``) del cliente ``subscriber_id`` -- mismo filtro.
